# Detection rules

<!-- Generated by `npm run docs:rules` from src/rules. Do not edit by hand. -->

Every finding carries a stable rule ID. Findings are **indicators**, not proof of a vulnerability: each one includes the evidence that triggered it so false positives are easy to investigate.

## MCP-001

**Protocol initialization failure** — default severity **critical**, category `protocol`, config key `rules.protocol`.

**What it detects.** The scanner could not connect to the server or complete the MCP initialize handshake.

**Why it matters.** A server that cannot initialize cannot be used by any MCP client, and nothing else about it can be verified.

**How to fix.** Run the server command by hand and check its stderr. For stdio servers make sure stdout carries only JSON-RPC messages (log to stderr). For HTTP servers confirm the URL, transport type and any required headers.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-001: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-002

**Invalid protocol version** — default severity **high**, category `protocol`, config key `rules.protocol`.

**What it detects.** The server negotiated a protocol version that is malformed or not supported by the MCP SDK.

**Why it matters.** Clients and servers must agree on a protocol version; an unsupported or malformed version causes undefined behaviour or refused connections.

**How to fix.** Respond to initialize with a date-formatted version the client requested or one you support (supported by this scanner: 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18, 2025-03-26, 2024-11-05, 2024-10-07). Upgrade your MCP SDK if it is old.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-002: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-003

**Invalid tool schema** — default severity **high**, category `schema`, config key `rules.schema`.

**What it detects.** A tool's inputSchema (or outputSchema) is missing, is not an object schema, is not valid JSON Schema, or contradicts itself.

**Why it matters.** Clients and models rely on the schema to build valid calls. An invalid schema makes the tool unusable or lets malformed input through.

**How to fix.** Give every tool an inputSchema of `{ "type": "object", "properties": {...}, "required": [...] }` that validates as JSON Schema, and make sure every `required` entry is defined in `properties`.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-003: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-004

**Prompt injection indicator** — default severity **critical**, category `security`, config key `rules.prompt_injection`.

**What it detects.** Server-provided text (tool descriptions, instructions, prompts, resources or tool output) contains phrasing that tries to override the model's instructions.

**Why it matters.** Anything an MCP server returns is read by the model. Embedded instructions can hijack the agent, leak data or trigger unwanted tool calls.

**How to fix.** Remove model-directed instructions from tool metadata and responses. Descriptions should say what a tool does, not tell the model how to behave. Treat tool output as untrusted data.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-004: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-005

**Tool poisoning indicator** — default severity **critical**, category `security`, config key `rules.tool_poisoning`.

**What it detects.** Tool metadata contains hidden or manipulative instructions: concealed tags, references to sensitive files, demands for side actions, exfiltration cues, tool shadowing, or invisible characters.

**Why it matters.** Users usually see only a tool's name. Hidden text in the description or schema can silently steer the model into reading secrets or sending data elsewhere.

**How to fix.** Keep tool descriptions short, factual and user-visible. Remove hidden tags, invisible characters and any text that references other tools, files or URLs. Pin and review tool definitions on every update.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-005: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-006

**Secret exposure** — default severity **high**, category `security`, config key `rules.secret_exposure`.

**What it detects.** Text from the server (descriptions, schema defaults/examples, instructions, tool output or stderr) contains what looks like an API key, token, password or private key.

**Why it matters.** Secrets published in metadata or logs are readable by every client, model provider and log collector that touches the server.

**How to fix.** Revoke and rotate the exposed credential, remove it from the source, load secrets from environment variables or a secret manager at runtime, and never echo them in output or logs.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-006: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-007

**Excessive permissions** — default severity **high**, category `security`, config key `rules.dangerous_permissions`.

**What it detects.** A tool can modify databases, read credentials, or make requests to arbitrary URLs, or the server bundles many high-impact capabilities.

**Why it matters.** The more a server can do, the more damage a confused or manipulated model can cause. Least privilege limits the blast radius.

**How to fix.** Split high-impact tools into separate, opt-in servers, scope each one to the minimum resources it needs (specific tables, hosts, paths), and set annotations such as readOnlyHint/destructiveHint.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-007: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-008

**Command injection risk** — default severity **high**, category `security`, config key `rules.command_injection`.

**What it detects.** A tool appears to wrap a command-line program and accepts unconstrained string arguments that could reach a shell or subprocess.

**Why it matters.** Values passed into a command line can inject extra arguments or shell metacharacters (`; rm -rf`, `$(...)`, `--flag`) when not validated or escaped.

**How to fix.** Invoke programs with an argument array (no shell), validate inputs with `enum`/`pattern`, reject values starting with `-`, and avoid string concatenation into command lines.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-008: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-009

**Missing timeout** — default severity **medium**, category `performance`, config key `rules.performance`.

**What it detects.** A tool hung past the timeout during an active scan, or (passively) a shell/database/network tool exposes no timeout, limit or row-cap parameter.

**Why it matters.** Tools that can run unbounded block the agent, hold connections and are an easy denial-of-service vector.

**How to fix.** Enforce a server-side timeout for every external call (database, HTTP, subprocess) and expose or document limits such as `timeout_ms`, `limit` or `max_results`.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-009: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-010

**Weak input validation** — default severity **medium**, category `schema`, config key `rules.schema`.

**What it detects.** A tool's input schema leaves parameters untyped, unbounded or free-form (e.g. an unconstrained `path`, `url` or `command` string).

**Why it matters.** Loose schemas let a model (or an attacker steering it) send unexpected values, which is the first step of most injection and path-traversal issues.

**How to fix.** Type every parameter, add `enum`/`pattern`/`maxLength`/`format` to strings, `minimum`/`maximum` to numbers, `items` to arrays, list `required` fields, and validate again on the server.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-010: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-011

**Dangerous filesystem operation** — default severity **high**, category `security`, config key `rules.dangerous_permissions`.

**What it detects.** A tool can write, modify or delete files, especially with an unrestricted path parameter.

**Why it matters.** Unscoped file writes allow overwriting configs, shell profiles or SSH keys; path traversal (`../`) can escape the intended directory.

**How to fix.** Restrict operations to an allowed root directory, resolve and verify paths server-side, require confirmation for deletes, and annotate the tool with destructiveHint.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-011: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-012

**Dangerous shell operation** — default severity **critical**, category `security`, config key `rules.dangerous_permissions`.

**What it detects.** A tool runs shell commands, scripts or arbitrary code.

**Why it matters.** Shell execution gives anything that can influence the model (prompt injection, poisoned content) full control of the host with the server's privileges.

**How to fix.** Avoid generic command execution. Expose narrow, purpose-built tools instead, or enforce an allowlist of commands and arguments, run in a sandbox/container with least privilege, and require human confirmation.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-012: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-013

**Missing tool description** — default severity **low**, category `tools`, config key `rules.quality`.

**What it detects.** A tool has no description.

**Why it matters.** Models choose tools by reading their descriptions. A tool with no description is rarely selected correctly.

**How to fix.** Write one or two sentences saying what the tool does, when to use it, and what it returns.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-013: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-014

**Duplicate tool** — default severity **medium**, category `tools`, config key `rules.quality`.

**What it detects.** Two or more tools (or resources/prompts) share the same name or URI.

**Why it matters.** Duplicate names make calls ambiguous: clients may call the wrong implementation or reject the whole list.

**How to fix.** Give every tool, prompt and resource a unique name or URI.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-014: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-015

**High tool latency** — default severity **medium**, category `performance`, config key `rules.performance`.

**What it detects.** A tool call, or tool discovery, took longer than the configured latency threshold.

**Why it matters.** Slow tools stall the agent loop and degrade the user's experience; very slow ones are often retried or abandoned by clients.

**How to fix.** Profile the tool, cache or paginate expensive work, stream progress notifications for long operations, or raise `thresholds.latency_ms` if the latency is expected.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-015: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-016

**Ping failed** — default severity **medium**, category `protocol`, config key `rules.protocol`.

**What it detects.** The server did not answer a `ping` request.

**Why it matters.** The MCP specification requires servers to respond to ping; clients use it for liveness checks.

**How to fix.** Handle the `ping` method and return an empty result object.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-016: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-017

**Unknown method not rejected** — default severity **low**, category `protocol`, config key `rules.protocol`.

**What it detects.** The server did not return a JSON-RPC error for an unknown method (it hung or returned success).

**Why it matters.** JSON-RPC requires an error (-32601 Method not found) for unknown methods. Hanging requests leave clients waiting until they time out.

**How to fix.** Make sure unrecognised methods produce a JSON-RPC error response. Most MCP SDKs do this by default; custom transports often do not.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-017: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-018

**Discovery request failed** — default severity **medium**, category `protocol`, config key `rules.protocol`.

**What it detects.** The server advertises a capability (tools/resources/prompts) but the corresponding list request failed.

**Why it matters.** If a declared capability cannot be listed, clients cannot use it and may treat the whole server as broken.

**How to fix.** Either implement the list method for each advertised capability or remove the capability from the initialize response.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-018: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-019

**Slow connection or initialization** — default severity **low**, category `performance`, config key `rules.performance`.

**What it detects.** Starting the server and completing initialize took longer than the latency threshold.

**Why it matters.** Clients start servers frequently; slow start-up delays every session and may hit client start-up timeouts.

**How to fix.** Defer heavy start-up work (index builds, downloads, auth) until the first call, or lazy-load dependencies. With `npx`, pin and pre-install packages.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-019: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-020

**Poor parameter descriptions** — default severity **low**, category `quality`, config key `rules.quality`.

**What it detects.** A tool has parameters with no description.

**Why it matters.** Parameter descriptions tell the model what to put in each field; without them models guess formats and units.

**How to fix.** Add a `description` to each property that states its meaning, format, units and an example value.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-020: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-021

**Inconsistent or invalid naming** — default severity **low**, category `tools`, config key `rules.quality`.

**What it detects.** Tool names use invalid characters, or mix naming conventions (snake_case, camelCase, kebab-case).

**Why it matters.** Clients may reject names outside [A-Za-z0-9_.-], and inconsistent naming makes the tool set harder for models and people to navigate.

**How to fix.** Use 1–128 characters from A–Z, a–z, 0–9, `_`, `-`, `.` and a single convention (snake_case is the most common).

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-021: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-022

**Excessive description length** — default severity **low**, category `quality`, config key `rules.quality`.

**What it detects.** A tool description is very long.

**Why it matters.** Long descriptions burn context tokens on every request and are where hidden instructions tend to hide.

**How to fix.** Keep descriptions under ~1,000 characters; move documentation elsewhere.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-022: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-023

**High timeout or error rate** — default severity **high**, category `performance`, config key `rules.performance`.

**What it detects.** In active mode, too many tool calls timed out or returned errors.

**Why it matters.** Frequent failures indicate an unreliable server; agents waste time on retries and may give up on the task.

**How to fix.** Check the failing tools' logs, add timeouts and retries for upstream calls, and return clear error messages for invalid input.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-023: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-024

**Missing tool annotations** — default severity **info**, category `tools`, config key `rules.quality`.

**What it detects.** Tools do not declare behavioural annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint).

**Why it matters.** Annotations let clients decide which calls need user confirmation. Without them clients must assume the worst.

**How to fix.** Set `annotations` on each tool, at minimum `readOnlyHint` and `destructiveHint`.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-024: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-025

**Unclear tool description** — default severity **low**, category `quality`, config key `rules.quality`.

**What it detects.** A tool's description is very short or just repeats its name.

**Why it matters.** Vague descriptions make it hard for a model to know when a tool applies and what it will do.

**How to fix.** Explain what the tool does, its inputs, side effects and what it returns, in plain language.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-025: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-026

**Excessive number of tools** — default severity **low**, category `quality`, config key `rules.quality`.

**What it detects.** The server exposes a very large number of tools.

**Why it matters.** Every tool definition is sent to the model on each request. Large tool sets burn context, slow responses and make wrong-tool selection more likely.

**How to fix.** Group rarely used tools behind a smaller set, split the server by domain, or let clients enable tools selectively.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-026: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-027

**Declared capability is empty** — default severity **low**, category `protocol`, config key `rules.protocol`.

**What it detects.** The server declares the tools, resources or prompts capability but lists none.

**Why it matters.** Clients show and plan around declared capabilities; an empty declaration is usually a configuration or registration bug.

**How to fix.** Register your handlers before connecting, or drop the capability from the initialize response if you do not use it.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-027: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-028

**Insecure transport** — default severity **high**, category `security`, config key `rules.dangerous_permissions`.

**What it detects.** A remote server is reached over plain HTTP instead of HTTPS.

**Why it matters.** Tool calls, results and any credentials in headers can be read or modified by anyone on the network path.

**How to fix.** Serve the MCP endpoint over HTTPS (TLS) and redirect or disable plain HTTP. Plain HTTP is acceptable only for localhost.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-028: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-029

**Missing server identity** — default severity **low**, category `protocol`, config key `rules.protocol`.

**What it detects.** The initialize response has no server name or version.

**Why it matters.** Clients and audit logs identify servers by name and version; without them, results and incidents cannot be attributed or pinned.

**How to fix.** Return `serverInfo: { name, version }` from initialize (MCP SDKs do this from the constructor arguments).

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-029: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-030

**Sensitive resource exposure** — default severity **high**, category `security`, config key `rules.dangerous_permissions`.

**What it detects.** A listed resource points at a sensitive location such as SSH keys, cloud credentials, .env files, or system password files.

**Why it matters.** Resources are readable by the model and, through it, by anyone who can influence the conversation. Credential files should never be exposed.

**How to fix.** Remove the resource, or serve a sanitised copy. Restrict file-backed resources to a dedicated, non-sensitive directory.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-030: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-031

**Network risk indicator** — default severity **medium**, category `security`, config key `rules.network_risk`.

**What it detects.** Server-provided text contains URLs or addresses that suggest data exfiltration or SSRF: known capture/tunnel hosts, URLs with templated data, image-embedded exfiltration, links to internal or cloud-metadata addresses, or non-HTTP schemes such as file:// and gopher://.

**Why it matters.** Text that points the model at external hosts is the standard way to move stolen data out (render an image, call a webhook), and internal addresses or odd URL schemes are the standard way to reach cloud credentials through a fetch tool.

**How to fix.** Remove external URLs from tool metadata unless they are documentation links users expect. Never let metadata or tool output instruct the model to call or render external URLs, and block internal/metadata addresses and non-HTTP schemes in any tool that fetches URLs.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-031: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```

## MCP-032

**Tool definition changed since baseline** — default severity **high**, category `security`, config key `rules.rug_pull`.

**What it detects.** Compared with the trusted baseline (mcp-detector.lock.json), a tool's description, schema or annotations changed, a tool was added, or the server instructions changed.

**Why it matters.** A server can behave well while you review it and later swap in malicious tool descriptions (a "rug pull"). Clients rarely tell you when a definition changes, so the only defence is to pin what you reviewed and alert on any difference.

**How to fix.** Review the change. If it is expected and safe, accept it with `mcp-detector pin`; if not, stop using the server and treat it as compromised. Commit mcp-detector.lock.json so changes show up in code review.

Disable or re-level it in `mcp-detector.yml`:

```yaml
rules:
  MCP-032: off      # or: low | medium | high | critical
```
